To give some context before the match the world champion was very concerned that he might lose his focus and end up losing a game, but other than that outside chance of some loss of face he was absolutely confident. As was most of everybody else. Even experts in the field felt AI was decades away from beating humans in Go. Chess is more fit for computers since it tends to be a more tactical game - calculation and 'board sight' are critical. Go is a more strategic game where intuition, experience, and 'feel' play a far greater role. Go also has a vastly greater branching factor.

The average chess position has about 35 legal moves, and in reality that can be heavily pruned pretty easily in most positions. By contrast in Go each position has an average of abut 250 possible moves - and pruning bad moves is much more challenging. And games in Go also tend to last much longer. The average chess game is about 40 moves. The average Go game is about 150 moves. To put some numbers to these values, just 10 moves in Go (10 moves for each player that is) would result in about 250^20 or about 10^48 possible games. The fastest supercomputer in the world can currently do 18 quadrillion floating point operations a second. Let's just say that evaluating a Go position is no more complex than a float point operation. It would take this computer 1,760,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 years to evaluate all those 10 moves.
